Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 specifies what types of property interests may and may not be transferred. It states that property of any kind may be transferred except in certain cases. These exceptions include: (a) mere chances of inheritance or legacy, (b) a mere right of re-entry for breach of a condition subsequent (only to the owner affected), (c) easements without the dominant heritage, (d) interests restricted to personal enjoyment, (e) rights to future maintenance, (f) public offices and salaries of public officers, (g) stipends and political pensions, (h) transfers that are contrary to the nature of the interest, unlawful object or consideration, or to a legally disqualified person, and (i) certain tenants, farmers, or lessees with untransferable rights cannot assign their interest as such. The section also clarifies that a mere right to sue or a public office cannot be transferred.

Section 7 of the Contract Act, 1872 requires that acceptance of a proposal must be absolute and unqualified. It also states that acceptance must be expressed in a usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal specifies otherwise. If the proposal prescribes a manner of acceptance and the acceptance is not made in that manner, the proposer may insist on the prescribed manner within a reasonable time; if they fail to do so, they are deemed to have accepted the acceptance in the manner given.

The Sindh High Court dismissed the criminal acquittal appeal filed by the appellant, upholding the acquittal of Respondent No.1 by the trial court. The court held that the trial court's decision was correct, particularly in view of the admitted fact that the complainant had legally handed over the house for renovation and that the accused had not committed any offence of theft or criminal breach of trust due to the absence of evidence and the benefit of doubt.

The final outcome in AHSAN v. The State (Cr.Acq.A. 124/2019) was that the appeal against the acquittal was dismissed in limine. The Sindh High Court held that the trial court's acquittal of the private respondent was not arbitrary or perverse, and that there were no glaring errors in the factual or legal findings. The court emphasized that interference with an acquittal is rare and requires a showing of perversity, grave misreading of evidence, or miscarriage of justice, which was not established in this case.

The application filed by the Province of Sindh to set aside the compromise decree was dismissed as misconceived and barred by limitation. The court examined whether the appellants were convicted under Section 149 PPC, which deals with the liability of members of an unlawful assembly, and whether the trial court provided a valid reason for awarding different penalties, particularly the death penalty, under Section 367(5) Cr.P.C., which requires a reason for imposing a penalty other than death.

The court also referred to judgments from the Supreme Court of Pakistan, including 2006 SCMR 50, 2006 SCMR 1304, and 2010 CLC 528, which provided guidance on the discretionary nature of revisional powers and the necessity of a failure of justice for interference.

The order of performance of reciprocal promises is governed by Section 52 of the Contract Act, 1872. If the order is expressly fixed by the contract, the promises must be performed in that order. If not, the order is determined by the nature of the transaction. For example, in a contract where one party promises to build a house and the other to pay for it, the building must be performed before payment. Similarly, if one party promises to deliver goods and the other to pay, delivery must occur before payment. As of 24 May 2023, the law in force is the Contract Act, 1872, and Section 52 applies to reciprocal promises regardless of the date, as it is a permanent provision of the Act.

The law on transfer of actionable claim applicable to the date of 11 September 2020 is governed by Section 130, 131, 132, and 136 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as these provisions are in force and do not specify a different version for that date. Under Section 130, the transfer of an actionable claim is effective upon execution of a written instrument signed by the transferor or his authorized agent, and the transferee acquires all rights and remedies of the transferor, including the right to sue in his own name, without needing the transferor's consent. Section 131 requires that notice of transfer must be in writing and signed by the transferor or his agent, or by the transferee or his agent, stating the name and address of the transferee. Section 132 imposes liability on the transferee, who takes the claim subject to all liabilities and equities that the transferor had at the time of transfer, including the right to set-off or other claims. Section 136 prohibits judges, legal practitioners, or officers connected with courts from buying or trafficking in actionable claims. These provisions are applicable as of 11 September 2020 unless otherwise modified by law, and no amendments to these sections are specified for that date in the provided documents.

If the accession is not capable of separate enjoyment or is necessary to preserve the property, the mortgagor is liable to pay the cost as an addition to the principal money with interest, and the profits from the accession are credited to the mortgagor. These provisions remain in force as of 17 September 2019.
